note: The h is silent. Works with anyone, any time.

lines.en: Hi, young man! What can I get you?

note: Until about noon. Say it when you walk into a shop, too.
Put it at the end of almost anything you ask for.
To get someone’s attention politely, before you ask a question.
Nobody minds. Say it with a smile and they’ll help.

lines.es: Son ciento ochenta y cinco pesos.

note: Your most useful phrase in the first months.

lines.es: Su cuarto está en el segundo piso.
lines.en: Your room is on the second floor.

note: Point at the thing and ask.

lines.en: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
At the back, on the right.

note: Quisiera… = I’d like… Swap in anything: quisiera un café.

lines.en: What would you like to drink?

note: In Mexico the check never comes until you ask for it.
The respectful way, for {mom}, {dad} and anyone older.
A warm step up from mucho gusto.
Friendly and firm with street sellers.

lines.en: Excuse me, do you speak English?

note: From about noon until dark.

lines.en: Good afternoon. What are you looking for?

note: After dark, both when you arrive and when you leave.
When you pass in front of someone or get up from the table.
¿Dónde está…? works for anything: el banco, el museo, la playa.

lines.en: Excuse me, where is the hotel?

note: Ask before you order: taco stands and markets are often cash only.

es: Me da dos tacos, por favor.
say: meh DAH dohs TAH-kohs, por fah-VOR
note: Me da… = Give me… It’s the normal, polite way to order in Mexico.

lines.es: Me da dos tacos, por favor.

note: Compliment the food early and often. It means a lot.
Say it to anyone eating, even strangers as you pass their table.
An attendant pumps the gas for you. Give 10 to 20 pesos as a tip.

lines.en: How much should I put in?
Good evening. I have a reservation.
And what do you do for work?

note: Point at anything. Great for learning words on the go.
Offer to help with dishes or setting the table. It wins hearts.
For an emergency anywhere in Mexico, call 911.
Agree on the price before the taxi starts, or use an app.
Also a normal goodbye in shops, even if you won’t be back.
A kind goodbye. With {sibling} or friends: que te vaya bien.
Claro que sí is even warmer.
Bounces a question back to {sibling} or friends. With {mom} and {dad} it’s ¿y usted?
Or name the word: ¿qué significa «botana»?
For real apologies and sad news. For a little bump, perdón is enough.

lines.en: I’m sorry, I got here late.

note: Shout it. The emergency number in Mexico is 911.
People light up when they hear this. Expect patience and help.
Your state comes from Settings → Nombres. For the country: soy de Estados Unidos.

lines.en: You’re not from here, are you?

note: With {sibling} or anyone your age: ¿de dónde eres?
The polite way. With {sibling}: ¿a qué te dedicas?

en: How do you say it in Spanish?
note: Say the English word first, then ask.

lines.en: Fork… how do you say it in Spanish?

note: Ya = already. They’ll keep offering food, so you’ll need this one. Pair it with estuvo delicioso.
When the meal is over. While you’re still eating, it’s ¡está delicioso!

lines.es: Ay, qué bueno que te gustó.
lines.en: Oh, I’m so glad you liked it.

note: When you raise a glass. Also what you say when someone sneezes.

en: Could you pass the salt, please?
say: meh PAH-sah lah SAHL, por fah-VOR
note: To {mom} or {dad}. With {sibling}: ¿me pasas la sal?

lines.en: Could you pass the salt, please?

note: Literally “I have hunger.” Thirsty works the same way: tengo sed.

es: Una mesa para dos, por favor.
say: OO-nah MEH-sah PAH-rah DOHS, por fah-VOR
note: Change the number: para tres, para cuatro.

lines.es: Una mesa para dos, por favor.

note: Locals know best. Works for food, places, anything.
Usually it isn’t. 10 to 15 percent is normal at restaurants.
Small shops often can’t break a 500-peso bill. Ask before you pay with one.

lines.en: I only have a five hundred. Do you have change?

note: Short and honest. A shrug helps.

lines.en: What time does my dad get here?

note: For surprise or disbelief. Your tone does the work.

lines.en: My mom made a hundred tamales.

note: Very Mexican. Nothing to do with fathers.

lines.en: Tomorrow we’re going to the beach.

note: Also a modest answer to “do you speak Spanish?”
Mexicans also say no pasa nada.

lines.en: Sorry, there are no enchiladas today.

note: For small things: a bump, squeezing past, interrupting.
You’ll hear it more than you say it, as in: al fondo, a la derecha.

lines.en: At the back, on the right.

lines.es: En la esquina, a la izquierda.
lines.en: On the corner, to the left.

note: Careful: derecho = straight, derecha = right. You’ll also hear siga derecho.
Agree on the price before you get in. Change the place: al centro, al hotel.
Tells the driver to stop here.
To {mom} or {dad}. With {sibling}: ¿cómo te fue?
Family comes first in Mexico. Asking this is always kind.

lines.es: Señora, tiene una casa muy bonita.
lines.en: Ma’am, you have a lovely home.
Thank you, sweetie. It’s your home too.

note: Trastes = dishes in Mexico. They’ll probably say no. Offer anyway.

lines.es: No, no. Yo lavo los trastes.
lines.en: No, no. I’ll do the dishes.

en: Thank you so much for having me.

lines.en: Thank you so much for having me.

es: Me gusta mucho la comida mexicana.
say: meh GOOS-tah MOO-choh lah koh-MEE-dah meh-hee-KAH-nah
note: Change the end: me gusta mucho el café, me gusta mucho aquí.

lines.es: ¡Sí! Me gusta mucho la comida mexicana.
lines.en: Yes! I really like Mexican food.

note: Change the thing: ¿le gusta el café? With {sibling}: ¿te gusta…?

lines.en: I love it! I’m a Chivas fan.

note: Literally “I have {age} years.” Your age comes from Settings → Nombres.

lines.en: And how old are you, dear?

note: Really tired: muy cansado.
Say it at the table. It tells them you’re glad to be there.

en: What time does the bus leave?
say: ah KEH OH-rah SAH-leh el ow-toh-BOOS
note: Long-distance buses in Mexico are comfortable and leave on time.

lines.en: What time does the bus leave?
Excuse me, where is the stop?

note: And to ask when they close: ¿a qué hora cierran?

lines.en: What time do you open tomorrow?

note: Y media = half past. Y cuarto = quarter past.
Parties run on relaxed time. Buses don’t.

lines.en: Should we go to the movies tomorrow?

lines.es: Sí. Nos vemos a las ocho.

note: Or call 911 yourself.
Change the thing: perdí mi cartera (wallet), perdí mi teléfono.

en: Would you let it go for 100?
note: Friendly bargaining is normal at markets, not in stores or restaurants.

lines.en: Would you let it go for a hundred?

en: I’d like to make a reservation.

lines.es: Quisiera hacer una reservación para el sábado.
lines.en: I’d like to make a reservation for Saturday.
Of course. For how many people?

note: A warm “my pleasure,” very common in Mexico after someone thanks you.
Said before grace or a family prayer. Many Mexican families say “Vamos a rezar.” Both are right.

lines.es: Antes de comer, vamos a orar.

note: Everyone says it together at the end of a prayer.

lines.en: Thank you for this family. Amen.

note: The start of the bendición de la mesa, the grace before meals. People often go on in their own words, then end with “Amén.”
Heard all the time in Mexico, for big things and small ones.

lines.en: Did you all get here okay?

note: Added to plans: “Nos vemos el domingo, si Dios quiere.”
Te is for tú: use it with {sibling} or anyone younger. With {mom} and {dad}, say “Dios lo bendiga” to him and “Dios la bendiga” to her.

lines.en: See you later. God bless you.

es: Padre nuestro, que estás en el cielo.
en: Our Father, who art in heaven.
say: PAH-dreh NWEHS-troh, keh ehs-TAHS ehn ehl SYEH-loh
note: The Padre Nuestro, one line a day. You speak to God with tú (estás), like family.

lines.es: Vamos a rezar el Padre Nuestro.
Padre nuestro, que estás en el cielo.
lines.en: Our Father, who art in heaven.

note: Santificado = honored as holy.

lines.es: Padre nuestro, que estás en el cielo.
lines.en: Our Father, who art in heaven.

note: Literally “may your kingdom come to us.”

es: Hágase tu voluntad en la tierra como en el cielo.
en: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
say: AH-gah-seh too boh-loon-TAHD ehn lah TYEH-rrah KOH-moh ehn ehl SYEH-loh

lines.es: Hágase tu voluntad en la tierra como en el cielo.
lines.en: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

es: Danos hoy nuestro pan de cada día.
en: Give us this day our daily bread.
say: DAH-nohs oy NWEHS-troh pahn deh KAH-dah DEE-ah
note: Pan de cada día = bread of each day.

lines.es: Hágase tu voluntad en la tierra como en el cielo.
lines.en: Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

lines.es: Danos hoy nuestro pan de cada día.
lines.en: Give us this day our daily bread.

es: Perdona nuestras ofensas, como también nosotros perdonamos a los que nos ofenden.
en: Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.
say: pehr-DOH-nah NWEHS-trahs oh-FEHN-sahs, KOH-moh tahm-BYEHN noh-SOH-trohs pehr-doh-NAH-mohs ah lohs keh nohs oh-FEHN-dehn
note: The longest line. Say it in two breaths: up to “ofensas,” then the rest.

lines.es: Danos hoy nuestro pan de cada día.
lines.en: Give us this day our daily bread.

lines.es: Perdona nuestras ofensas, como también nosotros perdonamos a los que nos ofenden.
lines.en: Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.

es: No nos dejes caer en la tentación, y líbranos del mal. Amén.
en: Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.
say: noh nohs DEH-hehs kah-EHR ehn lah tehn-tah-SYOHN, ee LEE-brah-nohs dehl MAHL. ah-MEHN
note: Literally “don’t let us fall into temptation, and free us from evil.” Some people say “caer en tentación,” without “la.”

lines.es: Perdona nuestras ofensas, como también nosotros perdonamos a los que nos ofenden.
lines.en: Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us.

lines.es: No nos dejes caer en la tentación, y líbranos del mal. Amén.
lines.en: Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.
